en: And drive off their mares from the hillsides;
Draw out all the ancient rage
Stored within the slaves.
Bring ruin upon their khan!
Exact your long-awaited vengeance!”
So saying, Aichürök
Set the half-dead, wretched slave’s
Soul ablaze,
Clothed him in the bulletproof coat,
Transformed his appearance completely,
And made him cast away
The felt coat he had worn in slavery.
Thinking the boastful warrior Kyyaz
Might come shouting upon them,
Or, if Choro rashly lost control,
That an axe might strike
The heroic Choro on the head,
And death might needlessly overtake
The weakened Choro—
Thinking it folly to overlook this,
His sister-in-law Aichürök
Showed her wisdom
And placed upon Külchoro’s head
A helmet of blue steel,
Pulling it firmly down.
There was no gap in the armor he wore;
Unless God had ordained death
For the orphaned Choro,
No mortal man could kill him.
From his sister-in-law, Külchoro
Received a fine bulletproof robe,
And, considering it, found the garment fitted well.
Then Aichürök
Dressed him in the bulletproof armor.
His precious sister-in-law Aichürök
Gave him honey when he thirsted,
Served him food at leisure,
And began entertaining conversation.
She had a fattened lamb and a savory head
Boiled until tender,
Heaped sugar white as snow,
Cut off chunks of yellow butter,
And filled his belly with tea.
His grief departed and joy arose;
Clad in bulletproof armor,
His painful ailments subsided,
His dimmed eyes opened,
His pent-up sorrow eased,
What had been broken was joined,
And what had scattered was gathered.
On seeing his sister-in-law, Külchoro
Became a full-grown lion once more;
He thrilled as strength filled his blood.
His head rose free from slavery,
His thirst was quenched and blood filled his veins—
Such was Külchoro’s condition.
AICHÜRÖK SHOWS SEYTEK
TO KÜLCHORO
Then Külchoro,
Whose wings had been clipped,
Who had lost his mighty lord,
Had passed his days in slavery
And withered in servitude.
Now his sister-in-law dressed him in fine clothes
And filled his soul with joy,
Yet the awaited moment seemed late:
To see Seytek, heir of the blue-maned wolf,
Just once, Choro’s
Two eyes yearned as though they were four.
His heart burned within him,
His arms had grown thin as reeds;
He longed to look upon
The orphan left by the hero—
This was now his dearest wish.
Burning with anguish and humiliation,
He felt the time long overdue
To see brave Seytek.
His senses reeled in helplessness,
The bones of his frame went slack;
His two eyes yearning as though they were four,
Külchoro stood staring imploringly.
This was why he implored:
The one who would support him climbing,
The one who would steady him descending,
The spring flowing down the hill,
The beloved of his sorrowing soul,
The young falcon left by the great-hearted hero.
His support in every trial,
The baby left by his mighty lord—
Could your hero die without seeing the child?
He was the wing on which Choro would circle and fly;
To see him once was
Külchoro’s consuming desire.
His heart burned like embers;
Enslaved and humiliated,
He longed to see just once
The child left by that fallen man.
His heart was pierced and torn,
His many torments rose before his eyes;
Overcome and distraught,
He readied himself like a hawk,
Found inspiration from the unseen,
And pleaded with Aichürök:
“My dear sister-in-law Aichürök,
Show to my eyes
The spring flowing through the valley,
The lamp left by the hero!
The plump gray falcon,
The morning star, the gray goshawk—
Bring him to me, sister-in-law,
That I may open my eyes and behold him,
Open my mouth and kiss him,
Press him to my breast,
And scatter all my sorrow!
Let this precious soul be born anew,
As though its former self had died;
Let Külchoro, your kinsman and khan,
Be as one newly born.
Let heroes race over hill and mountain;
Today let my fallen elder brother rise again!
Let the tears streaming down both cheeks
Pour to my skirts like a flood;
Let my swelling heart become a lake.
Today let long-buried Külchoro
Rise grandly like Ala-Too,
His sorrow gone, a warrior once again!
Let me bind Seytek, born of the hero,
Securely to my waist;
I shall confront brave Kyyaz
And exact payment for my heroic elder brother’s blood!
They raided my camp from Talas,
In hardship, misery, and dark disaster,
I am unable to take my revenge.
If the wound on my shoulder should heal,
If your towering Choro should recover,
Would I not sever the fated thread,
Would I not begin the upheaval?
Saying, “Choro has seized Kyyaz,”
I would begin the struggle,
I would make my fame known.
My belly boils, my heart burns—
Such is the state you see me in.
My strength is spent, my vigor gone—
I am as one already dead.
I, once an eagle, have become earth;
I, once a lion—alas, my head—
Have become a dug black grave:
Such is the state you find me in.
If you call this living, I count among no living men;
I am as one already dead.
Bring that dead soul back to life,
Show me your power as my sister-in-law.
While my mighty elder lived,
I was a keen warrior who scattered foes.
A bullet struck and pierced my chest,
And I cannot turn about.
My arm is broken, my leg disabled,
And I cannot rise to my feet.
Abandoned to the enemy’s scorn,
I cannot stand tall.
Carrying firewood on my back,
Fallen among a wrathful people,
I cannot show my face.
Karagul has become our master;
At his shout, we lose our peace.
My moon-bright sister Aichürök,
You have cast great turmoil among men.
Do not let your thoughts be divided;
Do not let them call him a stranger’s son,
The child born from your own body.
The seething Jediger—
Let me bring their proud banner down.
Kyyaz, son of Bagysh—
If my strength and power suffice,
Let me thrust his head into a pit.
If battle begins, let me do this:
Let me search every saddlebag
Of that sprawling swine;
Let me reap his grain while still green.
If fortune favors me, Kyyaz
I shall drive before me and torment.
Striking his mares out on the plain,
Let me smash his brains,
Take his camels as plunder,
And neatly slaughter his giant.
While splitting his belly like a donkey’s,
May my mind stay fixed upon the fool,
Until somehow I sever his head.
The man I fought was brave Kyyaz;
The man I sent flying was Semetey.
The one I must battle is Kanchoro;
The one I lost was Semetey.
My thoughts stray, sister-in-law,
To the torment suffered in humiliation.
My grief is vast, my anguish fierce:
May I die fighting.
I value my blood less than a spoonful;
For my khan and uncle, the gray-maned lion,
I shall spill every spoonful of my blood,
And spare my life not at all.
Kyyaz, son of Bagysh—
If only I might somehow beat the fury from him;
The Jediger who fill the Seven Valleys—
If only I might drive them all away;
If only I might slaughter their champions!
I have words to speak in tears,
A vengeance that will never leave my heart.
If I clash with him and raise a battle,
May that sprawling dog and I
Fall together where no one sees us.
For him she braided her hair in sorrow;
After long delay, she finally saw him.
When the figure before her
Came into view, her heart was content:
He was the gift she had longed for
From the gray-maned hero who had died.
The spring flowing down the hillside,
The young hero left by the magnanimous lord,
The banner held within her hand,
The precious legacy she had received
From the banner-winning hero.
Born after his mother came as plunder,
He would cast the whole world into tumult.
The time had come when God fulfilled her wish.
The moon waned and the days passed;
Many years went by.
Living out her days in grief,
Drinking water through a reed,
Brave Seytek had grown up in suffering:
The time had come when God fulfilled her wish.
This very year your young hero
Had reached the age of twelve.
Calling the Seven Valleys his homeland,
Separated from broad Talas,
Leaving wooded Talas behind,
Leaving the joyous Kyrgyz people,
Plundered and plunged into grief,
The ill-fated young hero, still in the womb,
Was bereft of his father
And fled to make the Seven Valleys his home.
Separated from his father,
He drew strength from his mother Aichürök;
That dear land of the Seven Valleys
He fittingly made his home,
And the Jediger of the Seven Valleys
He fittingly made his people.
Despised, he nevertheless prospered;
Fatherless, he grew to manhood;
Battered, he nevertheless came of age,
And ninety beasts were slaughtered for his feast.
I have made my sorrow into song—
Hear my lament, Aichürök!
Let me open my eyes and behold him;
Let me open my mouth and kiss him;
Bring me your only son!
If your only child is a true champion,
